Beyond the dashboard: The high cost of fragmented poverty data

Ben Brunckhorst

Minh Cong Nguyen

Nishant Yonzan

Sotaire Kwizera

July 23, 2026

This page in:

English

Poverty data are often scattered across separate surveys, making it difficult to identify how deprivations overlap and where policies can have the greatest impact. / Image: Shutterstock

Poverty is multidimensional, but measuring it that way is not easy. Data on some dimensions may not be collected in the first place due to budget constraints, conflict, or other barriers with no immediate solution. Or the data may exist but are fragmented across several datasets that are difficult to combine. For instance, we can estimate the share of low-income households from one dataset, those lacking basic infrastructure from another, and those with low education from a third – yet no single source captures all three dimensions together, making it difficult to know how deprivations overlap. This fragmentation is not just a technical inconvenience, it shapes what governments see, and therefore what they act on. Fragmented data leads to fragmented policies.
In what follows, we describe the fragmented state of poverty data and the cost of leaving those gaps unaddressed. Our companion blog outlines a method for combining datasets to measure multidimensional poverty in these scenarios.
 
The fragmented landscape of poverty data
While a wealth of household survey data exists for many countries, these datasets typically live in parallel, non-overlapping universes. For example, the World Bank’s Global Monitoring Database (GMD) captures income/consumption and basic demographics across more than 160 economies, while Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) capture demographic and health information of women and men of reproductive age across more than 90 economies. Accessing different data sources is costly, and even with access, combining them is not straightforward. They almost never sample the same households, making it impossible to link individuals across surveys.
A recent paper documents the gap in multidimensional poverty data, finding that only two indicators – educational attainment and phone ownership – are collected across four major cross-national survey databases: EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC), Gallup World Poll, Demographic and Health Surveys/Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (DHS/MICS), and Socio-Economic Database for Latin America and the Caribbean (SEDLAC). Figure 1, adapted from this paper and extended to include the World Bank’s GMD, illustrates how the global data landscape operates in thematic silos. To take one example, SDG 7 calls for universal access to electricity. However, the data on electricity access is available in four of the five databases. And where it is available, the overlap between lack of electricity access and any other deprivation can be observed for only 61 countries in Latin America and covered by EU-SILC, representing less than 8 percent of the global population.
 
Figure 1: No single database gives the full picture

 
What fragmented data hides
Consider what we learn when looking at deprivation across a single dimension, multiple separate dimensions (a dashboard view), and an overlapping view of those dimensions.

Figure 2. Seeing the overlap reveals what a dashboard can miss

Let's look at an example of single and multidimensional view of poverty using Angola's data in 2018. A single dimension view shows us nearly 2 in 5 people live on less than $3/day (2021 PPP). The dark dots are the share in poverty while the lighter dots are those not in poverty.This is a crucial starting point as there is a lot of overlap between monetary poverty and other forms of poverty. However, monetary poverty alone does not capture all poor households.A dashboard view broadens the poverty picture: alongside monetary poverty, nearly 1 in 3 lack adequate education and more than 2 in 3 lack basic infrastructure. However, the dashboard can be misleading. It tells us how many people face each problem individually but tells us nothing about whether they are the same people facing multiple deprivations at the same time.A multidimensional view shows a more complete picture. It is not just that millions are lacking infrastructure and education, but nearly a fifth of the population face all three deprivations (income, education, and infrastructure) simultaneously.

 
Getting it wrong can be costly
Fragmented data leads to inefficiencies, increased costs, and policy gaps. When critical overlaps are invisible, ministries often act separately: hiring different contractors, running separate procurement processes, and duplicating fixed delivery costs. Seeing overlapping deprivations changes the economics: bundled infrastructure, shared fixed costs, and “dig once” delivery can help the same investment reach more households. For instance, consider that the most cost-effective education policy might actually be an energy policy. If most children dropping out of school live in homes without electricity, unable to study after dark, or attend schools without power, then connecting those households to the grid may do more for enrollment than building new classrooms. Without knowing that these are the same children, that insight is entirely lost.
Fortunately, there are solutions. A recent paper highlighted in a companion blog  introduces a method to combine aggregate statistics from fragmented data to measure multidimensional poverty. These methods, among others, can help policymakers better understand overlapping deprivations, reduce inefficiencies, and make better-informed decisions to end poverty.
